stories.title: Is Mouthwash Secretly Bad For You? Scientists Check the Rumour
stories.headline_kid: Some people online said mouthwash could harm your body — so scientists checked if it's actually true.
summary: You probably brush your teeth every morning and night. Some people also swish mouthwash around their mouth afterwards to make their breath fresh. But recently, posts online claimed that mouthwash could kill the 'good' bacteria in your mouth and even cause serious health problems like diabetes and heart disease.

That sounds scary! So a group of experts, including a professor who studies mouths and gums, looked closely at the science to see if these claims were true. Your mouth is home to millions of tiny bacteria, and most of them are actually helpful, not harmful.

The good news is that the experts found no strong proof that using mouthwash once in a while — like once a week or once a month — hurts most people. They said the worry mostly applies to using very strong mouthwash every single day for a long time without a dentist's advice.

This story is a good reminder that not everything you read on social media is completely true. It's always smart to check with a trusted adult, doctor, or dentist before believing a scary health claim online.

lenses.me: You can keep using mouthwash normally without worrying, as long as you don't overdo it every single day.
lenses.family: Your parents might have seen this claim online too — you can help by sharing what scientists actually found.
lenses.friends: If your friends talk about scary health rumours, you can help by asking 'is this actually proven?'
lenses.nation: Singapore's health experts often remind people to check facts before believing viral health claims.
lenses.world: This shows how quickly health myths can spread worldwide through social media, even without proof.

stories.title: No, Singapore Did NOT Discuss the Death Penalty With Israel
stories.headline_kid: Singapore's government has firmly corrected a false rumour about a recent visit by Israeli officials.
summary: Israel's security ministry recently visited Singapore. After the visit, some rumours spread online claiming that the two countries had talked about the death penalty — a serious punishment where a criminal's life is taken away for very serious crimes.
Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) quickly stepped in to correct this. They said the death penalty was 'never part of the meeting and was not discussed' at all.

Instead, MHA explained that the real topics were about sharing 'best practices' — meaning good, proven methods — in things like emergency response, stopping crime, and forensics. Forensics is the science detectives use to solve crimes, like checking fingerprints or footprints, similar to what you might see in a detective show.

This story shows how important it is for governments to correct wrong information quickly, before it confuses or worries people. It's also a useful reminder for all of us to check facts before believing something we read online.

lenses.me: It teaches you to always double-check facts before believing a rumour, even ones about serious topics.
lenses.family: Your family might discuss how governments handle safety and crime prevention together with other countries.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates can talk about how easily false information can spread online.
lenses.nation: Singapore's government values being clear and truthful with the public about important matters.
lenses.world: It shows how rumours about one country's meeting can quickly spread and cause confusion internationally.

stories.title: Nepal Needs Nearly S$6.5 Billion to Rebuild After Deadly Floods
stories.headline_kid: Rebuilding homes, roads and bridges after last month's terrible Nepal floods will cost an enormous amount of money.
summary: Last month, a huge chunk of a glacier — think of it as a giant block of mountain ice — broke off in Nepal and crashed down, sending a massive wall of water, mud and debris rushing through villages like a tsunami. It was one of the worst disasters Nepal has faced in years.

On Friday, Nepal's foreign ministry announced that rebuilding everything that was destroyed will cost about US$4.78 billion — that's roughly S$6.4 billion! This money is needed to fix homes, roads, bridges and other things families need every day.
Sadly, rescuers have now recovered 1,385 bodies, and around 5,130 people are still missing. Many families are still waiting anxiously for news of their loved ones.

Singapore has been checking in on nearly 100 Singaporeans who were in Nepal when the disaster struck, since some Singaporeans love trekking in Nepal's beautiful mountains. This shows how a disaster far away can still touch people close to home.

lenses.me: It helps you understand how natural disasters can destroy not just homes, but also change entire communities.
lenses.family: Your family might discuss ways to help, like donating to disaster relief funds for Nepal.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates could organise a small fundraiser to help children affected by the floods.
lenses.nation: Singapore has strong ties with Nepal and continues to check on Singaporeans affected by the disaster.
lenses.world: This disaster highlights how melting glaciers, possibly linked to climate change, can cause deadly floods worldwide.

stories.title: A Group Just Took Over an Important Sea Route — Here's Why Singapore Cares
stories.headline_kid: A group called the Houthis has taken control of a key stretch of sea, and this could affect ships and prices around the world.
summary: Imagine a narrow hallway that every ship carrying oil and goods must pass through to reach the rest of the world. That's what a 'strait' is — a narrow strip of sea connecting two bigger bodies of water. Singapore itself sits next to a famous one, the Singapore Strait!

In Yemen, a group called the Houthis has just seized control of the entire Red Sea coast, along with three important islands. This area is close to a strait that thousands of cargo ships use every year to carry goods and oil between Asia, Europe, and beyond.

This takeover could make shipping through the area more dangerous or difficult, which may cause delays and push up the cost of oil and other goods. Since Singapore is one of the busiest ports in the world and relies heavily on smooth global shipping, any trouble at sea can eventually affect prices here too.
Experts are watching closely to see how this situation develops, since ongoing conflict in the region has already been affecting oil prices in recent weeks.

lenses.me: Things you buy, like snacks or toys, could become slightly pricier if shipping costs rise.
lenses.family: Your family might notice higher petrol or grocery prices if this trouble at sea continues.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can discuss how something happening far away can still affect Singapore.
lenses.nation: Singapore's economy depends heavily on ships moving safely and smoothly through world seas.
lenses.world: This affects global trade, oil supplies, and prices for countries everywhere, not just in the Middle East.

stories.title: Meet the Singaporean Making Storybooks Every Child Can Enjoy
stories.headline_kid: A former lawyer in Singapore now creates special storybooks so children with different abilities can enjoy reading together.
summary: Lee Seow Ser used to work as a lawyer, but during a break from her job, she found a new passion: making children's books that everyone can enjoy, no matter their ability. Together with two other women, she started a project called 'To SIR (Socially Inclusive Reads) With Love'.

Their books include special features like braille, which are raised dots that blind or visually impaired people can read with their fingers. They also add tactile pictures — images you can feel with your fingers — and use dyslexia-friendly text, which is easier to read for children who find letters tricky to recognise.

The goal is simple but powerful: to make sure children of all abilities can enjoy the very same stories at the very same time, rather than feeling left out. The team also holds events to help other children understand and appreciate people with disabilities and special needs.
This heartwarming initiative shows how one person's small idea, sparked from wanting to give back, can grow into something that brings joy and inclusion to many families across Singapore.
